candidates.title: How Public Evals Work, Where They Break, and What Should Change
candidates.author: Eugene Yan
candidates.organization: eugeneyan.com (author is Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic)
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-22 (article:published_time 2026-11-22T00:00:00Z; RSS pubDate Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000; date-only, no real time)
candidates.what_changed: A 42-minute teardown of 12 public agent benchmarks (Terminal Bench, DeepSWE, FrontierSWE, Terminal Bench Science, GDPval, Harvey LAB, AutomationBench, Agents' Last Exam, Finance Agent, HealthBench Professional, BrowseComp, OSWorld 2.0) with concrete grader-failure counts and recommendations on how practitioners should read and build evals.
candidates.mechanism: Decomposes eval tasks into instruction / environment / grader / optional reference; catalogs design principles (deterministic checks over LLM judges, outcome-not-steps grading, all-pass vs partial credit, difficulty mining); quantifies grader false negatives (unstated requirements, hidden tests clashing with agent-written tests, wrong answer keys) and false positives (string-contains assertions, rubric items that only check presence); argues for pass^k reliability, human-attention cost instead of dollar cost per task, multi-turn evals, negative tests (do-nothing and adversarial agents), transcript audits, and evaluating models inside your own production harness.
candidates.evidence_quality: High for a secondary synthesis: cites specific audit numbers from benchmark papers, Epoch AI reviews, Preference Model rebuild, Artificial Analysis, and the author's own review of dozens of failed DeepSWE trajectories. Several figures are attributed to third-party audits not re-checked here (UNVERIFIED beyond the post).
candidates.independent_confirmation: Partial. Latent Space AINews (2026-11-21) separately reports METR's finding that swarms overfit to self-generated tests and that horizons are longer on easy-to-verify tasks, consistent with the verification-gap theme. Individual audit numbers (e.g., 41/65 TBench 4.0 tasks on unstated requirements, >60% hallucination in Harvey LAB passes) not independently confirmed here: UNVERIFIED.
candidates.relevance: Very high. Directly actionable for anyone choosing models off leaderboards or building internal evals: add pass^k, audit tasks where several frontier models fail the same check, add do-nothing/adversarial negative tests, audit passing transcripts, avoid string-contains assertions, measure review/redo time rather than token cost, and benchmark inside your own harness.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to Edition 3's 'production cost per user vs eval cost per task' and 'verifying agent done claims' themes (the post explicitly argues cost-per-task is misleading and that agents declare false success). Materially new: grader-error audit data across 12 benchmarks and concrete grader-hardening techniques. Frame as 'how to read/fix evals', not a repeat of cost or done-claim verification.
candidates.summary: Eugene Yan studied 12 public evals and found evidence in 8 of them that the grader failed work that should have passed. Task anatomy: instruction (single-shot, no clarifying questions), environment (container/VM/docs), grader (code assertions, LLM judge on binary rubric, or both), optional human reference. Benchmarks now ship like software: Agents' Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57; Harvey LAB's public set grew from ~1,250 to 2,010 tasks since May 2026; Terminal Bench drops saturated tasks per version, breaking cross-version comparison. Principles: deterministic checks over LLM judges (DeepSWE and AutomationBench use none); grade outcome not steps; all-pass scoring is common (Harvey: 'no partial credit for catching most of the issues') but brittle; difficulty mining (BrowseComp kept only questions strongest models failed; HealthBench Professional made hard tasks ~3.5x more common). Model failure modes: skipping verification / stopping early (OSWorld 2.0, Harvey LAB, AutomationBench agents summarized partial lists as done) and dropping stated requirements (most common GDPval failure). Grader false negatives: 41 of 65 Terminal Bench 4.0 tasks graded on unstated requirements (Preference Model rebuild; making them explicit lifted one model from 63% to 89%); Epoch AI found scoring defects in 30 of 66 TBench tasks, 11 failing correct solutions; 23 of 113 DeepSWE tasks marked correct solutions as failures, and Epoch found hidden test files clash with agent-written tests in 18 of 113 tasks (penalizing agents that verify their own work), with an audit finding correct solutions failed in at least 20% of DeepSWE v1.1 tasks; OSWorld 2.0 had checks failing correct work in 23 of 108 tasks; BrowseComp trainers disagreed with the reference answer on 50 of 367 (14%); Terminal Bench Science has 128 task-fix issues on 57 of 70 tasks (79 verifier/instruction bugs), e.g. a verifier rejecting correct predictions in a different row order, and one run got 99 of 100 stars right and scored zero. False positives: Artificial Analysis found material hallucinations in >60% of Harvey LAB results that passed every criterion; 55% of AutomationBench assertions only check string contains/excludes (an email swapping counts '3' and '4' would pass); 44 of 65 Terminal Bench v4 tasks could be passed by cheating. Recommendations: report pass^k (two agents at 70% average: one reliable on 70% of tasks stays 70% at k=5, the other drops to 17%); cost per task misleads because models fail cheaply (17% of Agents' Last Exam failures were premature abandonment; on FrontierSWE one model submitted and stopped within 8 of 20 hours in 169 of 170 trials; on AutomationBench models declared success on 72-91% of analyzed failures; GDPval showed GPT-4o at ~1/10 GPT-5's cost per task but slower than an expert alone once review/redo time was included); verifiable tasks test implementation more than judgment (FrontierSWE's self-check tool spoon-feeds what to measure); real work is multi-turn (Laban et al.: 39% lower scores in simulated multi-turn); invest in graders: audit tasks where multiple frontier models fail the same check, add negative tests (do-nothing agent, adversarial agent), audit passing transcripts for reward hacking (FrontierSWE judge panel). Scores reflect model+harness: on Terminal Bench 2.0 one model scored 57.8% on neutral Terminus 2 vs 52.1% on its provider's harness, another 32.6% vs 19.6%; takeaway: evaluate models inside your own production harness. Also: FrontierSWE v2 switched from wall-clock to weighted instruction count for deterministic perf grading; author suggests scoring 1 - 1/speedup instead of capping at a target, and publishing partial credit alongside all-pass. GDPval human graders agreed 71% of the time; grader model agreed with them 66%.

candidates.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
candidates.author: Richard MacManus
candidates.what_changed: Survey/interview piece on AI-driven formal verification vendors (&Truth, Harmonic, Theorem, Axiom Math) as a way to check agent-written code, featuring &Truth co-founder Clark Barrett (cvc5 co-creator).
candidates.mechanism: LLMs generate proofs that a checker (Lean, or Rocq in Anthropic/Theorem's work) verifies step by step; SMT solvers like cvc5 used for spec analysis and test generation (e.g., in Amazon's Kiro); 'veri-coding' workflow where the developer nails down a spec with the agent and the agent collaborates with a verification tool under the hood.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium-low: journalistic interview plus vendor claims; one quantitative datapoint attributed to an Anthropic/Theorem post (Opus 5.5 reached 50% solve rate on 36 small verification tasks with ~40% fewer tokens than Opus 5) not checked at source (UNVERIFIED).
candidates.independent_confirmation: None checked for the token-efficiency figure. cvc5-in-Kiro and 'billions of calls a day at Amazon' are Barrett's statements: UNVERIFIED.
candidates.relevance: Medium. Conceptually relevant (verification as the answer to agent output quality) but little that a practitioner can configure this week; no hands-on recipe. Possible brief or context for an evals/verification story.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Thematically near 'verifying agent done claims' and 'harness-enforced checks'; different mechanism (formal proofs vs host records).
candidates.summary: Frames 2026's word of the year 'slop' and proposes formal verification as a defense. Clark Barrett (&Truth co-CEO, Stanford, cvc5 co-creator) says cvc5 is used for spec analysis and test generation in Amazon's Kiro and is 'called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon.' Contrasts agent 'verification' (tests, self-critique, LLM judges) with proof: 'how do you know when you're done' — testing never tells you if one more issue lurks. &Truth builds a Lean-based 'verification machine' and &Atlas, a map of open-source C code; key use case is proving memory safety across C codebases. Mentions GPT-6.2 Astra producing a Lean proof of Smoktunowicz's Gap Theorem (per Vals), Anthropic formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem (13M lines), Levent Alpöge's Claude-assisted Riemann Hypothesis claim posted as Lean. Axiom Math uses verification as training feedback (AxiomProver, AXLE toolkit); Harmonic's Aristotle: 'AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step.' Theorem + Anthropic post 'LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale': on 36 small verification tasks, Opus 5.5 reached 50% solve rate with ~40% fewer tokens than Opus 5 (diagram uses Rocq). 'Veri-coding': developer time shifts to spec writing and review. Closes with Cognition's Nader Dabit on 'outcome engineering'.

Most actionable: try Inkling 2 Mini locally (GGUF/Ollama/vLLM) as a small open coding model; the LoRA-concatenation harness adapter recipe; Cloudflare Clairic for self-hosted invoice extraction; Gemini server-side tool search. Mostly needs primary-source follow-up by other slices.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: GrepMem (append-only log + regex, 95-97% on ContextBench vs <=21% lossy) overlaps Edition 3's agent memory/grep logs topic. Gemini 4 Neon was covered in the prior Latent Space issue already reviewed. Rest is new.
candidates.summary: Lead: Anthropic's Levent Alpöge claims a Claude-assisted proof of RH/GRH released only as Lean (1.3GB, ~250,000 page-equivalent); Elliot Glazer confirms the formal statement is GRH and puts a Lean bug at <<1%, compile still running; work began Oct 6, final 'GRH' entry Nov 16; model and degree of steering undisclosed. Masullo released a 940-page, 12-year human proof the same day. swyx contrasts 'probably correct but incomprehensible' vs 'probably technically incorrect but understandable' and ties it to slop and weak-to-strong alignment. ANT stock fell ~10%. Inkling 2 Mini (Thinking Machines): 26.4B looped MoE, Apache 2.0, AA Index 20.1, DeepSWE v1.1 48.2%, Vals Index 46.5%, ties Opus 5.5 on CyberBench at <1/4 cost (Vals), ARC-AGI-2 49.3% at $0.14/task; GB200 TP1 decode 10.29 -> 3.84 ms at batch 1; ~75 tok/s on DGX Spark (Soumith), 'roughly as good as Qwen 3.8 27B'; Unsloth reports ~90% top-1 retention even at 1-bit. Gemini 4 Neon: Company Agent Bench 87.4%, FrontierCode 2.0 46.2% vs Opus 5.5 47.3% at $4.38 vs $12.82/task; subscriptions reportedly usable in any harness from Dec 2. METR Time Horizons 2.0: doubling 3.6 months, GPT-6 Astra 40.3h, Opus 5.5 39.0h (wide CI); horizons longer on easy-to-verify tasks; larger agent swarms overfit to self-generated tests. MIT CSAIL paper argues context offloading, programmatic tool calls and sub-agents keep LLM calls in-distribution; surrogate harness training. HF harness super-adapter (rank-96 from three LoRAs) lifts SWE-Bench Pro hard 45->61% (Hermes), 47->67% (OpenCode), 19-48% fewer tool calls. GrepMem 95-97% on ContextBench. Hyperstition judge-time scaling: Fable 5.2 as token-level editor judge closed 68% of Qwen2.5-7B base-to-Instruct gap on MATH with ~1% of GRPO tokens. Tencent Hy4 770B/49B-active open weights; Hy4-flash 156B-A12B. Microsoft MAI Code 2 claimed 96% of Opus 5.5 at 5% cost. Cloudflare released Apache-2.0 Clairic (Qwen3.8-27B-based) and Clairic-flash (Qwen3.5-9B) for invoice/receipt extraction with typed fields, confidences and spans. Anthropic IPO $81.3B raised at $83/share.

candidates.title: Pre-training is (still) not plateauing
candidates.author: Sebastian Raschka
candidates.event_date: 2026-11-22 (references OpenAI post 'Perplexity and Intelligence', date not checked: UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Quick note highlighting OpenAI's 'Perplexity and Intelligence' chart showing held-out code log-perplexity keeps falling from GPT-4 to GPT-4.5 and later base models.
candidates.mechanism: Explains log-perplexity as average negative log probability of each target token (cross-entropy); frames pretraining = knowledge, post-training (SFT + RLVR) = access to knowledge, harness = application of knowledge.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low-medium: short commentary on a single OpenAI chart; Raschka notes it is a next-token metric, not task success, and wants a FLOPs x-axis.
candidates.independent_confirmation: OpenAI source linked (https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/) but not fetched here: UNVERIFIED.
candidates.relevance: Low-medium for applied readers: useful explainer of perplexity as a metric; little to configure. Could support a brief if another slice covers the OpenAI post.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Low; Raschka's Nov 17 LR-decay note was used previously (different topic).
candidates.summary: Raschka cites OpenAI's 'Perplexity and Intelligence' (described as rare transparency from a closed lab) showing lower log-perplexity on held-out code from GPT-4 to GPT-4.5 and later base models, as evidence pretraining is not plateauing, just 'boring' relative to RLVR and harness engineering. Walkthrough: for 'I really like chocolate', feed 'I really like', take the probability of 'chocolate', negative log, average over targets = cross-entropy = log-perplexity. Caveats: metric is next-token prediction not task success, though it correlates with perceived real-world performance; he wants the same plot vs training FLOPs. Expects labs to keep investing in pretraining, e.g., tuning the code fraction of the training mix.

candidates.title: The US-China Open-Weight Feedback Loop
candidates.author: Sebastian Raschka
candidates.what_changed: Quick note (originally Substack Notes) with a timeline figure and reference table of architecture ideas crossing between US and Chinese open-weight models, 2021-2026.
candidates.mechanism: Lineage table: LLaMA <- RoFormer RoPE; DeepSeek LLM 67B <- Google GQA; OLMoE <- DeepSeekMoE fine-grained experts; DeepSeek-V3 <- Meta multi-token prediction; Kimi K2 <- DeepSeek-V2 MLA; Qwen3-Next <- Gated DeltaNet hybrid attention; Trinity Large <- Qwen gated attention sigmoid gate; Instella-MoE <- MLA + output gating; Marin Mochi <- Jianlin Su's quantile balancing for router bias.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium: accurate-seeming architectural lineage, opinion framing ('competition is good').
candidates.independent_confirmation: Not checked: UNVERIFIED for 2026 entries (Trinity Large, Instella-MoE, Marin Mochi).
candidates.relevance: Low for 'try this week'; background reading on architecture components.
candidates.summary: Raschka argues US open-weight models wouldn't be as good without Chinese ones and vice versa, and proprietary models wouldn't be as good or cheap without open-weight models. Figure plus table of borrowed ideas: RoPE (RoFormer -> LLaMA), GQA (Google -> DeepSeek LLM 67B), fine-grained experts (DeepSeekMoE -> OLMoE), multi-token prediction (Meta -> DeepSeek-V3), MLA for KV-cache compression (DeepSeek-V2 -> Kimi K2), Gated DeltaNet hybrid attention (-> Qwen3-Next), learned sigmoid attention output gate (Qwen -> Arcee Trinity Large), MLA + output gating (AMD Instella-MoE), quantile balancing router-bias adjustment (Jianlin Su -> Open Athena Marin Mochi).
